title: Match the piece, then the tops decide

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the top number of 3/8 turn from 3 to 6 while its shaded run stays put, so the tops, 6 against 5, agree with the runs, when you count both in sixteenths.
interactive.title: Count both in one piece
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Two bars of the same length, one above the other with their left ends in line, each one whole: call each an inch, as the last lesson did, so the two fractions are of the same whole. The upper bar is cut into eight equal pieces with the first three shaded as one run, labelled 3/8: the 3/8 bit. The lower bar is cut into sixteen equal pieces with the first five shaded, labelled 5/16. Beneath both runs one number line, 0 under the left ends and 1 under the right, with a mark under the end of each run, labelled 3/8 and 5/16. The stepper chooses the piece both bars are counted in. At the opening setting, each in its own piece, nothing is renamed and the readouts give 3 and 5, each fraction's own top number. Step to sixteenths and cuts appear inside every eighth of the upper bar, its label changes to 6/16 and its readout to 6, while its run and its mark stay where they were; the lower bar is already in sixteenths, so it does not change. At thirty-seconds both bars gain cuts and read 12/32 and 10/32; at sixty-fourths, 24/64 and 20/64. The third readout is the gap between the two marks, 0.0625 of an inch at every setting.

The rule is the last lesson's renaming, done to both fractions with one piece in mind. The new piece must measure each run exactly, so the chosen bottom number has to be a whole number of times the old one: 16 ÷ 8 = 2, so each eighth is cut into 2 sixteenths and the upper top becomes 3 × 2 = 6; 16 ÷ 16 = 1, so the lower bar is cut into 1, which is no cut, and its top stays 5 × 1 = 5. In general each readout is that bar's own top number × (chosen bottom ÷ its own bottom): at thirty-seconds, 3 × 4 = 12 and 5 × 2 = 10; at sixty-fourths, 3 × 8 = 24 and 5 × 4 = 20. Neither mark moves, because each renaming cuts every piece into the same number of smaller pieces and multiplies the count by that same number, as the last lesson showed: 3/8 is 3 × 0.125 = 0.375 of the whole and 5/16 is 5 × 0.0625 = 0.3125 at every setting, so the gap is 0.375 − 0.3125 = 0.0625, one sixteenth of the inch. Once both bars are counted in one piece the tops can be read against each other: 6 against 5, 12 against 10, 24 against 20, the bigger top on the longer run every time, and the gap between the marks spans 1 piece at sixteenths, 2 at thirty-seconds and 4 at sixty-fourths, the same length each time.
interactive.ignores: The bars answer the question before the counting does: the 3/8 run is visibly the longer from the start. The renaming is how you get that answer from the two names alone, with no bars drawn, which is the case at the drill box. The stepper offers only pieces that measure both runs exactly, so it never shows the choice going wrong: counted in eighths, the 5/16 run would end halfway through a piece, with no whole number to read, and tenths measure neither. Both bars are one inch, so this is a comparison of two fractions of the same whole; 3/8 of a metre against 5/16 of an inch is a comparison of lengths these bars do not show. Cuts and marks are drawn with no width, so the runs end on exact places; a real drill bit is made to a tolerance and a tape's marks have a width. Two fixed drill sizes are drawn; the same steps compare any pair of fractions of one whole.

explain.text:
Which drill bit is the bigger, 3/8 or 5/16? Read as pairs of whole numbers, 5 beats 3 and 16 beats 8, and neither comparison settles anything, because the two fractions are counted in different pieces: eighths of an inch against sixteenths of it. Give both fractions the same piece and the question becomes a plain count: the top numbers then count pieces of one size, and the bigger count is the bigger bit. Remember from the lesson before last that a sixteenth is half an eighth, because sixteen of them make the same inch that eight eighths make, and from the last lesson that cutting every piece into the same number of smaller pieces renames a fraction without moving it? Those two facts are the whole method.

Counting compares like with like. Three drums against five drums is a fair comparison; three metres against five millimetres is not, until both are in one unit. A fraction's top number is a count and its bottom names what is being counted, so two tops can be compared only when the two bottoms match; a bottom number that two fractions share is what textbooks call a [[common denominator]], denominator being the bottom number's long name from the second lesson. **To compare two fractions of the same whole, rename both in one piece that measures each exactly, and then the bigger top is the bigger fraction.**[^1] Sixteenths measure both of these bits: 16 ÷ 8 = 2 comes out whole, so each eighth is two sixteenths and 3/8 is 3 × 2 = 6 sixteenths, 6/16, the renaming from the last lesson, which keeps the fraction's value;[^2] and 16 ÷ 16 = 1, so 5/16 is already counted in sixteenths. Six sixteenths against five: 3/8 is the bigger bit, by one sixteenth of an inch. The line beneath the bars agrees: 3/8 sits at 3 × 0.125 = 0.375 and 5/16 at 5 × 0.0625 = 0.3125, and 0.375 − 0.3125 = 0.0625 is one sixteenth. The tops can be trusted now and not before for two reasons. The renaming moved neither mark, because the piece shrank by exactly the factor the count grew, so 6/16 sits at the same point on the line as 3/8 and is the same number;[^3] and once both runs are built from pieces of one size, the run with more pieces is the longer, as surely as six tails of one length laid end to end outrun five.

Why sixteenths and not eighths? An eighth does not measure 5/16 exactly: 8 ÷ 16 is not a whole number, so the 5/16 run would end halfway through an eighth, with no whole count to read. A piece measures a fraction exactly when the fraction's bottom goes into the new bottom a whole number of times, and sixteenths are the coarsest piece that both 8 and 16 go into. Finer ones work too, which is what the stepper shows: at thirty-seconds the bars read 12/32 against 10/32, at sixty-fourths 24/64 against 20/64, the same order and the same gap each time, because the renaming never moves a mark. When no shared piece is obvious, multiplying the two bottoms gives one that both go into,[^4] and renaming each fraction by the other's bottom keeps both values:[^5] 8 × 16 = 128, so 48/128 against 40/128, correct, only finer than it needs to be. Matching the piece is one of several ways to compare fractions,[^6] and it is the one to keep because it works for any pair of the same whole.

The habit that fails here is the whole-number habit from the last two lessons: people who study how fractions are learned list judging a fraction by its whole numbers, taking 1/5 as more than 1/2 because 5 is more than 2, among the common errors,[^7] and by it 5/16 looks the bigger bit, since both its numbers are bigger. On the bars it is the shorter run: its 5 counts sixteenths, each half an eighth, so five of them make two and a half eighths, short of the three that 3/8 counts. The bigger-bottom rule from the lesson before last does not rescue the comparison either: it is the test for fractions whose tops match,[^8] and 3 and 5 do not. So comparing the tops needs matching bottoms, comparing the bottoms needs matching tops, and for a pair like 3/8 and 5/16, where neither matches, renaming is what makes the bottoms match. One check comes before all of it: comparing fractions is only valid when both refer to the same whole,[^9] so 3/8 of an inch against 5/16 of an inch is a fair question and 3/8 of an inch against 5/16 of a metre is not, however the pieces are matched.

**To compare two fractions of one whole, rename both in a piece that measures each exactly, and then the bigger top is the bigger fraction: in sixteenths 3/8 is 6 against 5/16's 5, so it is the bigger bit.[^1][^9]**

analogy.text: Say a control circuit carries a 500 mA fuse and a plug carries a 3 A fuse. As bare numbers 500 beats 3, but a milliamp and an amp are different-sized pieces of current, a thousand milliamps to the amp, so the two counts are not comparable as they stand. Put both in milliamps, 3 × 1000 = 3000 against 500, and the bigger count is the bigger fuse. That is the lesson's move: one piece first, then the counts decide.
analogy.breaks: With units the piece is fixed by the prefix, a thousand for milli, so there is no piece to choose; with fractions you choose the piece, and it has to measure both exactly, which is the check 16 ÷ 8 = 2 does. And units let you go the other way, 0.5 A against 3 A, because a decimal can count half an amp; a fraction renamed needs a whole count, so a coarser piece that leaves half a piece over is no use.

practice.text:
Deciding which of two fractions is bigger (drill sizes, spanner sizes, shares of an hour):
- Check both are fractions of the same whole: the same inch, the same hour, the same drum. If not, stop: the comparison is not valid.
- Bottoms already the same? The bigger top is the bigger fraction. Done.
- Tops already the same? The bigger bottom is the smaller fraction, from the lesson before last. Done.
- Otherwise choose a piece that measures both: try the bigger bottom first, and check that the smaller bottom goes into it a whole number of times (16 ÷ 8 = 2: yes). If it does not, multiply the two bottoms together; that piece measures both every time.
- Rename each fraction into that piece: multiply its top and its bottom by the number its bottom needs to reach the chosen one.
- Now compare the tops. The difference between them is how much bigger, counted in the chosen piece.

**Rule of thumb:** same piece first, then the tops. The bigger bottom as the trial piece; the two bottoms multiplied as the piece that never fails.

**Worked example:** a drawing calls for a clearance hole no bigger than 3/8 inch, and the bit in your hand is stamped 11/32. Same whole, an inch. Bottoms differ, tops differ. Try the bigger bottom: 32 ÷ 8 = 4, whole, so thirty-seconds measure both. 3/8 is 3 × 4 = 12 thirty-seconds, 12/32; 11/32 is already there. 11 is less than 12, so the 11/32 bit is the smaller, by one thirty-second of an inch: it is within the limit. For a pair where neither bottom goes into the other, say 2/3 of an hour against 3/4 of an hour, multiply the bottoms: 3 × 4 = 12, twelfths. 2/3 is 2 × 4 = 8 twelfths and 3/4 is 3 × 3 = 9 twelfths, so three-quarters of an hour is the longer, by one twelfth of an hour, which is 60 ÷ 12 = 5 minutes.

**Common mistakes:**
- Comparing the tops while the bottoms differ: 5/16 taken as bigger than 3/8 because 5 beats 3. The 5 counts smaller pieces. Match the piece first.
- Using bigger-bottom-means-smaller when the tops differ. It settles 3/8 against 3/16, where both tops are 3; it does not settle 3/8 against 5/16.
- Choosing a piece that measures only one of them: eighths for 3/8 and 5/16 leave 5/16 at two and a half eighths, no whole count. Go finer, to a piece both bottoms go into.
- Renaming by adding: 3/8 made into 11/16 by adding 8 to top and bottom has moved, from 0.375 to 0.6875. Multiply top and bottom by the same number, as the last lesson showed.
- Renaming only the bottom: 3/8 written as 3/16 is a different, shorter length. The top is multiplied by the same number as the bottom.
- Comparing across wholes: 3/8 of an inch against 5/16 of a metre is not a comparison of fractions at all; put both lengths in one unit and compare the lengths.
- Treating the renamed fraction as a bigger one: 6/16 is 3/8, the same length; it has more pieces because they are smaller.
